title: The Value of Stories in Business | Aswath Damodaran | Talks at Google
description:
The world of investing/finance is divided into two camps. In one, you have the number-crunchers, who believe that the only things that matter are the numbers and that imagination/creativity are dangerous distractions. In the other, you have the storytellers, who build on the stories they tell about companies and how these stories will bring untold wealth. Each side believes it has a monopoly on the truth and looks with contempt at the other. Prof. Damodaran contends that stories matter, but only if they are connected with numbers. And numbers are empty, unless they are connected with narratives. In this talk, he looks at the process by which one might build narratives, check them against reality and convert them into valuations. Uber and Ferrari examples are used to illustrate the process.

Slides for the talk: https://goo.gl/zKVaQL

Check out the book on Google Play: https://goo.gl/tnGlDe

This talk was moderated by Saurabh Madaan.
summary: The talk argues that consistent storytelling allows markets to grant significant slack to companies like Amazon even during long periods without profits. It further contends that accounting definitions often fail to capture the true value of tech giants like Google and Meta, suggesting that R&D should be capitalized rather than expensed. Additionally, the speaker highlights that the online advertising market is dominated by two giants who capture almost all profits, while noting that reputation risk can be a fatal flaw, as seen with Valeant.

claims.claim: The speaker identifies Intel as a tech company and a cash cow, but does not express a specific investment view on it in this passage.
claims.quote: Intel is tech, but so is Facebook and so is Snap. But what do they share in common? One is a company that's I mean, not quite the walking dead, but if you think about Yahoo, so you can have walking dead tech companies which are essentially looking towards the exit and you can have companies growing.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker identifies Microsoft as an example of an 'old tech' company that represents a bargain in the market.
claims.quote: So in tech companies, I think we need to stop talking tech as a collective space and think about some of the best bargains in this market are in the old tech space. I'm talking the Microsofts, the Intels. These are cash cows.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker lists McDonald's as a consumer product company that can be disrupted, implying it is subject to the same risks as tech companies.
claims.quote: Can be disrupted? Sure. So can GM, so can Ford, so can Coca-Cola, so can McDonald's. What makes us think that just because you have a consumer product company, I can't disrupt you? Disruption is part of this process.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker states that accounting definitions fail to capture what is needed to grow a company like Google, specifically regarding R&D and buying young technologies.
claims.quote: And what do accountants do with it? Screw it up big time, right? They treat it as an operating expense. And if I ask a company like Google, what do you have to reinvest to grow, you can already see the accounting definitions are not going to capture what you put money in to grow.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker argues that for a company like Google, R&D must be capitalized rather than treated as an expense to properly value the company.
claims.quote: My invested capital at a company like Google will require me to capitalize R&D, right? Because if you put money in R&D and I do what the accountants do, it will never shop as--
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Warren Buffett bought Apple, which he views as a small step given his previous reluctance to buy tech companies.
claims.quote: I was happy when Warren Buffett finally bought Apple because it's a small step, but for a long time his view was, I don't buy tech companies. In fact, his view was, I don't buy anything I don't understand.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: Amazon is a counter-example where telling a consistent story allows markets to cut the company significant slack despite long periods without profits.
claims.quote: To me Amazon is the perfect counter-example of if you can tell a consistent story, markets will cut you a heck of a lot of slack. You know why they don't do it for most companies? Because the story keeps changing every year.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: Tesla is an example of a company needing external capital that is more valuable if priced higher to issue stock cheaply and cover cash burn.
claims.quote: So there are some companies that need external capital at the beginning, like Tesla, right? For those companies, they're actually more valuable if they are priced higher because the capital will be very low, right?
claims.speaker: AUDIENCE

claims.claim: The speaker missed the damage to Valeant's reputation and assumed it would become an old-fashioned drug company, but it did not.
claims.quote: I assumed that they would become an old fashioned drug company. But to become an old fashioned drug company, what do you have to do? You have to build an R&D department, you've got to hire scientists.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker describes Uber as a matchmaker business that collects a 20% fee from fares, noting that drivers use it to earn a second income legally.
claims.quote: For essentially being matchmakers, they collected 20% of whatever you pay. I said, this is a great business. Which left me with one missing piece, why do customers like Uber?
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran

claims.claim: Uber's aggressive, rule-breaking culture is both a strength that enabled success and a potential weakness that could lead to failure, as bad guys sometimes win in business stories.
claims.quote: Uber has this combination of being aggressive-- they've always been an aggressive company that's broken every rule in the book and they've succeeded with it. But in a sense, it's also their biggest weakness.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: Google is one of only two giants in online advertising that dominate profits, making it a highly profitable business despite industry consolidation.
claims.quote: The only thing is there are only two giants in the room sucking up all the profits-- one is you, the other is Facebook. For the rest of the world, it's become a bad business.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: Facebook (Meta) is one of only two giants in online advertising that dominate profits, driving 60% of growth in the business and making it a profitable but skewed market.
claims.quote: The only thing is there are only two giants in the room sucking up all the profits-- one is you, the other is Facebook. For the rest of the world, it's become a bad business.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: Facebook's ability to show direct attribution of clicks to purchases makes it easier for advertisers to understand value compared to other platforms.
claims.quote: I think it's easier for you than it is for Facebook, for instance, because you have a search engine that people go through. It's much more direct to say, this is how you landed on a site is through us.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The online advertising business is profitable but skewed, with Google and Facebook capturing almost all profits while others like Twitter struggle to show profits despite having revenues.
claims.quote: So it is a profitable business, but it's a very skewed profit. The two companies at the top get almost all of the profits, the rest don't even get the droppings off the table. They're like Twitter, they basically have revenues but they can't show profits.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker lost 60% of their investment because the company damaged its reputation so severely that it became impossible to be a going concern.
claims.quote: So what I missed in the case of Valeant is the damage that they had done to their reputation that makes it almost impossible for them to be a going concern. That damage cost me, what, 60% of my investment in Valeant.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker bought Apple in 1998 as a charitable contribution, but had to sell portions of the position due to price increases, leaving half the profits on the table.
claims.quote: I bought Apple in 1998 and I bought it as a charitable contribution. Because I loved Apple so much. It looked like it was going out of business and this was going to be my final contribution, look how much I loved you. Here, take the $14.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker bought Apple four times and sold it four times in the last six years because the market price fluctuates wildly based on product cycles and investor sentiment.
claims.quote: I've bought Apple four times and I've sold Apple four times in the last six years. Why? Because my value stayed stable, but here's what happens to Apple. A new iPhone comes out, revenues jump 8%, people start dancing in the streets. It's a growth company again.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker sets a trigger point to buy Apple only when the stock is at least 80% undervalued relative to their distribution of value, which would be around $124 to $122.
claims.quote: So I'm not going to buy Apple when it drops to $139. My value is $140. It dropping to $139, I'm still with-- if you look at this distribution, I'm so close to my expected value. So by having a distribution, I can look up a trigger point and say-- and I have to set the trigger.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker bought Apple at $94 and put a limit sell order at $140, which executed, resulting in Apple being out of their portfolio.
claims.quote: When I bought Apple, I got lucky. I bought Apple at $94, I put a limit sell at $140, and it executed so Apple is out of my portfolio.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker bought Volkswagen after its value dropped 24% because they believe the issues affecting Volkswagen are common across the entire industry.
claims.quote: That's why I bought Volkswagen after the-- because I looked at Volkswagen and said, hey, do you think only Volkswagen does this stuff? They all do it. You've knocked down the value of Volkswagen 24%.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker considers buying United after it dropped a billion dollars because it is a damaged company in an industry where all companies are damaged.
claims.quote: So would I buy United after the billion dollars? Maybe. Here's why. It's a damaged company, but it's in a business where they're all damaged.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker suggests that Delta might have dragged the airline industry down even more than United did, implying the industry is broadly damaged.
claims.quote: There but for the grace of God goes Delta, right? Don't assume that Delta would not have dragged you off. Maybe they'd have dragged you off a little more gently, OK?
claims.speaker: ASWATH DAMODARAN
